messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sophie Müller was 28 when the incident happened, a patrol officer who had still believed, up to that point, that whatever strains came with the job were held together by trust inside the unit. During a night response to a chaotic street stop, she found herself caught in a crush of shouting, flashing lights, and bodies moving too fast to read. An officer she knew well swung his baton while she was trying to pull a handcuffed man back from the curb; in the confusion, Sophie was struck hard and driven to the pavement as other officers piled in. What stayed with her was not only the pain and the sound of boots scraping asphalt, but the instant of looking up and seeing the face of someone from her own department above her while force continued around her. The scene made no sense to her even as it happened. She had gone into policing with the assumption that danger came from outside and that her own team was where safety lived. In the weeks after, she could not shake the conviction that she had been betrayed by people she was trained to rely on, and that if this could happen in uniform, under lights, surrounded by colleagues, then the world was dangerous in a way she had failed to understand.

Those beliefs did not remain abstract. Sophie had come to see her own body as an enemy, something that kept surging into alarm without her permission. A spike in her heart rate, a tightening in her chest, the jolt in her shoulders when she heard raised voices at work all seemed to prove to her that she was not actually safe anywhere, because even when nothing was happening her body behaved as though the assault were beginning again. That sense of being under threat made the memory harder to keep in the past. Standing in the station hallway and hearing radios crackle, or catching the chemical smell of wet pavement and sweat after a call, she would abruptly be back on the ground with the same sensory force: the glare of emergency lights, the pressure of weight above her, the noise coming from every direction at once. The memory forced itself into her mind when she did not want it to, and because she already believed the world was unsafe and trust could collapse without warning, these intrusions arrived less like recollections than like confirmation that danger was present now.

When the memory came, it felt completely real across all her senses. She did not experience it as “thinking about” the event; she felt herself in it, as if the station corridor or patrol car had dropped away. At times she would grip the edge of her desk and stare, trying to reorient, unsettled by how little the experience felt like an ordinary memory. Just as disturbing, afterward it could seem strangely alien, as though it belonged to someone else rather than to her, a scene she had been forced to witness rather than a part of her own life. Yet this very strangeness fed the meanings she had drawn from the assault. If her own mind could turn on her like that, if her body could launch into panic and her memory could seize control without warning, she took it as evidence that she had been fundamentally changed by what happened and could not rely on herself any more than she could rely on other people.

Over the following months, these reactions became woven into her workdays. As a police officer she could not avoid uniforms, radios, shouted commands, or the hard fluorescent corridors of precinct life, and each exposure carried the risk of being pulled back into the scene. She became watchful around fellow officers, scanning tone, posture, and sudden movements for signs that force could erupt again. The more she noticed her body lurching into readiness, the more certain she became that danger was everywhere and that betrayal was not an exception but a fact she had been naïve enough to miss. In turn, the intrusive reliving hit with greater force, arriving in the locker room, in the passenger seat between calls, sometimes when her partner at home touched her unexpectedly and she had to remind herself where she was.

By the time she sought help, Sophie was exhausted by living in a state that felt both hyperreal and unreal. She could describe the incident in fragments, but the most vivid parts still broke in on her rather than feeling fully like hers to tell. What finally brought her in was the fear that she was losing any solid sense of safety, at work and outside it, and that her own body would keep dragging her back into that night no matter where she was. More than anything, she wanted to know whether it was possible to stop feeling ambushed by her own reactions and to trust, even cautiously, that the world was not only the place where she had been hurt.
